specPoints.text: practical: investigate thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation

primer.text: Three experiments, three transfer routes. Metal strips and dropping ball bearings rank conductors; a purple dye trail films a convection current in water; four differently painted flasks turn surface finish into cooling curves. Together they put conduction, convection and radiation on the bench.

lessons.title: Experiment 1: conduction in four metals
lessons.opening: Four metal strips meet at a heated centre, each carrying a ball bearing stuck on with wax at the same distance out. The wax lets go in conduction-speed order: the first bearing to drop hangs on the best conductor, and the falling order ranks copper, aluminium, brass and iron.
keyPoints: The aim is to rank four different metals by how quickly they conduct heat along their length.
The independent variable is the type of metal; the dependent variable is the rate of conduction.
Control variables include the size and thickness of the strips, the amount of wax and identical ball bearings.
Ball bearings are attached with wax; when conducted heat melts the wax, the bearing drops, and the drop time is recorded.
The first bearing to fall marks the best thermal conductor; the observed order is copper, then aluminium, then brass, then iron.

low.restatement: Heat the shared centre of four metal strips, time how long each strip’s wax takes to release its ball bearing, and read the conductivity ranking straight off the falling order.
low.analogy: Four runners handed a relay baton at the same instant: the finishing order is the conducting order.
low.examPointer: Controls earn marks: equal strip size and thickness, equal wax, identical bearings — otherwise the comparison is unfair.

medium.restatement: Better conductors push heat along their length sooner, so their wax reaches melting temperature first; repetition and averaging steady the timing.
medium.analogy: A row of candle wicks of different materials lit from a shared flame: some carry the flame to their far end before the others.
medium.examPointer: Quote the expected order if asked: copper (fastest) > aluminium > brass > iron (slowest).

check.stem: What is the independent variable in experiment 1?

options.text: the time taken for the bearing to drop
options.explanation: That is the dependent variable.

options.text: the type of metal strip
options.explanation: Four different metals provide the input.

options.text: the amount of wax
options.explanation: Wax amount is a control variable.

options.text: the flame size
options.explanation: The flame is kept gentle and consistent — a control.

check.stem: What makes each ball bearing fall?

options.text: the bearing is pushed by expanding metal
options.explanation: The release is the WAX melting, not a push.

options.text: conducted heat melts the wax holding it
options.explanation: The wax releases when conduction warms it to melting.

options.text: the bearing slides off the tilted strip
options.explanation: The strips are horizontal; nothing slides until release.

options.text: the bearing evaporates the wax
options.explanation: Bearing cannot evaporate anything.

check.stem: The first ball bearing to fall is on the strip that is:

options.text: the worst thermal conductor, because it holds heat longest
options.explanation: Holding heat is not conducting it.

options.text: the best thermal conductor, because heat reached the wax fastest
options.explanation: Fast conduction melts the wax first.

options.text: the heaviest metal
options.explanation: Density is not the tested variable.

options.text: the one farthest from the flame
options.explanation: All strips meet at the same heated centre.

check.stem: Which control variable list matches the method?

options.text: strip size and thickness, amount of wax, identical ball bearings
options.explanation: These are the declared controls.

options.text: flame size, room temperature, time of day
options.explanation: The declared controls are the strip/wax/bearing set.

options.text: type of metal, wax amount, time
options.explanation: Metal type is the independent variable and time the measurement.

options.text: no controls are needed
options.explanation: A fair test needs the declared controls.

check.stem: The copper bearing falls at 45 s and the iron bearing at 210 s. What does the comparison show?

options.text: copper conducted the heat to its wax faster than iron
options.explanation: 45 s is far less than 210 s, so copper’s wax melted first.

options.text: iron is the better conductor because its time is bigger
options.explanation: A longer time means SLOWER conduction.

options.text: copper’s wax was thinner
options.explanation: Wax amount is controlled, so that cannot explain it.

options.text: the result is impossible
options.explanation: Copper is the known best conductor of the four.

check.stem: State the dependent variable of experiment 1.
check.modelAnswer: The rate of conduction, measured by the time taken for each ball bearing to drop.

check.stem: State the expected conductivity order of the four metals from the results.
check.modelAnswer: Copper first (best conductor), then aluminium, then brass, then iron last.

check.stem: Explain why the ball bearings must be attached at an equal distance from the centre on every strip.
check.modelAnswer: The comparison is only fair if the heat must travel the same distance before melting each blob of wax: a nearer bearing would drop sooner regardless of the metal, so equal distances keep the metal type as the only thing being tested.

check.stem: A student repeats the experiment with a silver strip added. Predict where silver falls in the falling order relative to copper, and justify the prediction.
check.modelAnswer: Silver conducts slightly better than copper, so its bearing would be expected to fall first, marginally ahead of copper; the ranking logic is that better conductors melt their wax sooner.

lessons.title: Experiment 2: convection in water
lessons.opening: A crystal of potassium permanganate drops into water and bleeds purple. Warm the water gently right below it and the purple trail becomes a movie of the convection current: rising above the flame, spreading, cooling, sinking and circling back — in cold water and warm water alike, at different speeds.
keyPoints: The aim is to investigate the rate of convection using potassium permanganate crystals in two temperatures of water.
The independent variable is the temperature of the water; the dependent variable is the rate of convection.
Controls include the amount of water, the size of the Bunsen flame and the size of the crystal.
The crystal is dropped carefully into the centre of the beaker of water and the beaker is heated gently below it.
The purple trail traces the convection current, and the trail’s speed shows the rate of convection in each water temperature.

low.restatement: The dye rides the current: warm water rises above the flame carrying the purple trail, cools, sinks at the edges and returns, and the loop runs faster in warmer water.
low.analogy: Ink dropped into a lazy river bend: the ink is passive, the flow draws the picture, and the flow’s speed is the story.
low.examPointer: The crystal is the MARKER, not the mover — say the water’s motion carries it, or you lose the mechanism mark.

medium.restatement: Controls keep the current’s shape comparable: same water volume, same flame, same crystal size — so the only real difference is the water’s starting temperature and hence the convection rate.
medium.analogy: Two identical go-kart tracks with different starting speeds: the tracks must match before you compare the laps.
medium.examPointer: Careful handling earns marks: forceps for the crystal, gentle heating, not-too-full beaker — quote them as method points.

check.stem: What is the role of the potassium permanganate crystal in experiment 2?

options.text: it heats the water
options.explanation: The Bunsen flame heats the water.

options.text: it is a visible marker whose trail shows the convection current
options.explanation: The purple trail traces the water’s motion.

options.text: it reacts to warm the water chemically
options.explanation: No chemistry drives the current.

options.text: it colours the flame
options.explanation: The crystal colours the WATER, not the flame.

check.stem: What is the independent variable in experiment 2?

options.text: the temperature of the water
options.explanation: Two starting temperatures of water are compared.

options.text: the rate of convection
options.explanation: That is the dependent variable.

options.text: the size of the crystal
options.explanation: Crystal size is controlled.

options.text: the beaker volume
options.explanation: Water amount is controlled.

check.stem: Where should the crystal be dropped, and why?

options.text: at the edge, so it dissolves faster
options.explanation: The edge is not the observation point.

options.text: in the centre of the beaker, carefully, so the trail forms cleanly above the heating point
options.explanation: The centre placement puts the current where it can be seen.

options.text: on the bottom of the beaker before adding water
options.explanation: The crystal drops into the water by forceps.

options.text: in the flame directly
options.explanation: The crystal goes into the WATER.

check.stem: The purple trail above the flame moves upward fastest. Why does it rise?

options.text: the dye is lighter than water and floats
options.explanation: The trail follows the WATER’s motion.

options.text: the warmed water has expanded and become less dense, so it rises carrying the dye
options.explanation: The density chain is the mechanism.

options.text: the flame blows the water upwards
options.explanation: A gentle flame below the beaker does not blow the water.

options.text: the crystal dissolves only upwards
options.explanation: Dissolution is not directional.

check.stem: The convection current is faster in the warm-water beaker. What does that comparison demonstrate?

options.text: warmer water convects faster, so the rate of convection rises with temperature
options.explanation: That is the experiment’s conclusion.

options.text: the dye dissolves faster in warm water
options.explanation: Dissolution rate is not the measured quantity.

options.text: cold water cannot convect at all
options.explanation: It convects more slowly, not never.

options.text: the flame was bigger in the warm beaker
options.explanation: Flame size is controlled.

check.stem: State the dependent variable of experiment 2.
check.modelAnswer: The rate of convection, observed through the speed of the purple convection current.

check.stem: State three control variables of experiment 2.
check.modelAnswer: The amount of water in the beaker, the size of the Bunsen flame and the size of the potassium permanganate crystal.

check.stem: Explain why the beaker must not be filled to the brim.
check.modelAnswer: A convection current needs room to complete its loop: water must rise above the heating point, cross the surface and sink at the sides. A brim-full beaker spills when the water moves and leaves no free surface for the return leg, spoiling both the observation and the safety of the set-up.

check.stem: The purple trail takes 12 s to complete one loop in warm water and 30 s in cold water. Compare the convection rates and state what the experiment demonstrates.
check.modelAnswer: The warm-water loop completes in 12 s against 30 s in cold water, so convection is about two and a half times faster there; the experiment demonstrates that the rate of convection increases with the water’s temperature.

lessons.title: Experiment 3: radiation from different surfaces
lessons.opening: Four identical flasks — black, dull grey, white and silver — filled with the same hot water at the same starting temperature, then timed with thermometers. The black flask cools fastest, the silver slowest, and the temperature-time curves put the emit-and-absorb law of surfaces on the page.
keyPoints: The aim is to test how a surface’s nature sets how much infrared it absorbs and radiates.
The independent variable is the colour of the flask; the dependent variable is the temperature of the water.
Controls keep the flasks identical apart from their finish, with equal hot water, one shared starting temperature and one shared timing interval.
Temperatures are recorded at regular intervals, for example every 30 seconds for 10 minutes.
The black flask cools fastest and the silver flask slowest, matching the emit-and-absorb ranking of surfaces.

low.restatement: Same water, same start, four finishes: the cooling curves order themselves black first, then grey, then white, then silver last — the emission ranking drawn in temperature.
low.analogy: Four identical mugs of tea in winter, one painted black, one wrapped in foil: the paint job decides who cools first.
low.examPointer: Quote the control set — identical flasks except colour, same volumes, same start temperature, same intervals — before quoting the ranking.

medium.restatement: The cooling rate is the emission rate made visible: steeper early drop for black, flattest for silver; the evaluation adds heatproof mats, thermometer resolution of 1 °C and repeat runs.
medium.analogy: Four runners of the same fitness on different shoes: the shoes — like the surfaces — set who crosses the line first.
medium.examPointer: Safety and evaluation: hot water scalds, mats protect the bench, and repeats average out reading scatter at ±1 °C resolution.

check.stem: What is the independent variable in experiment 3?

options.text: the temperature of the water
options.explanation: Temperature is the dependent variable.

options.text: the colour of the flask
options.explanation: Four colours provide the input.

options.text: the time interval
options.explanation: Intervals are controlled.

options.text: the amount of water
options.explanation: Water amount is controlled.

check.stem: Which flask’s water cools fastest?

options.text: the silver flask, because shiny surfaces reflect heat inwards
options.explanation: Reflecting inward is not the behaviour here; shiny emits poorly, so it cools SLOWEST.

options.text: the black flask, because black surfaces are the best emitters
options.explanation: Best emission means fastest radiative cooling.

options.text: the white flask, because white reflects light
options.explanation: White is a poor but not the poorest emitter.

options.text: all cool at the same rate
options.explanation: The surface finish decides the rate.

check.stem: Which set of control variables matches the method?

options.text: flasks identical apart from their colour, equal hot water, one shared starting temperature, shared timing intervals
options.explanation: These are the declared controls.

options.text: different flask sizes so each colour is visible
options.explanation: Flasks must be identical except colour.

options.text: different water depths per colour
options.explanation: Water amounts must match.

options.text: no controls are needed
options.explanation: The fair test depends on the controls.

check.stem: After 10 minutes the black flask reads 52 °C and the silver flask reads 61 °C, both from 80 °C. Which statement is correct?

options.text: the black flask lost 28 °C and the silver 19 °C, so black radiated more
options.explanation: 80-52 = 28 and 80-61 = 19; the bigger drop is the bigger emitter.

options.text: the silver flask lost more because it ended hotter
options.explanation: Ending hotter means it LOST less.

options.text: both lost the same because they started the same
options.explanation: Same start does not mean same loss.

options.text: the black flask gained energy
options.explanation: Both cooled; neither gained.

check.stem: Why does the flask experiment investigate RADIATION rather than conduction or convection?

options.text: because water only loses energy by radiation
options.explanation: Water loses energy by all three routes; the design isolates the surface effect.

options.text: because the flasks are identical except for their surface finish, so the surface’s radiating behaviour is the tested factor
options.explanation: Isolating the surface isolates the radiative route.

options.text: because convection cannot happen in water
options.explanation: Water convects freely.

options.text: because thermometers measure radiation directly
options.explanation: Thermometers measure temperature.

check.stem: State the dependent variable of experiment 3.
check.modelAnswer: The temperature of the water in each flask, recorded over time.

check.stem: State the resolution of the thermometers used in experiment 3.
check.modelAnswer: The thermometers read to 1 °C, so temperatures are recorded to the nearest degree.

check.stem: Explain why all four flasks must start at the same temperature.
check.modelAnswer: The hotter an object, the faster it radiates, so a flask starting warmer would cool faster for that reason alone. Equal starting temperatures make the surface finish — not the initial energy content — the only thing setting each cooling rate.

check.stem: A silver-coated emergency blanket wraps a runner after a race. Explain whether wrapping the SHINY side inward is the right choice.
check.modelAnswer: Yes: the shiny surface is a very poor emitter, so turned inward it radiates the runner’s body heat away at the slowest rate, and its reflectivity bounces radiation back toward the body — exactly the behaviour wanted to retain warmth.

glossary.definition: The apparatus holding four metal strips meeting at a heated centre, used to rank thermal conductors.
The purple crystal whose dissolving trail makes the convection current visible.
How well a material conducts heat; high conductivity heats up faster along its length.
The smallest change an instrument can record, such as 0.01 s on the stopwatch or 1 °C on the thermometer.
